content: Upon admission, the WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist recommends the following steps: 1. Assess for danger signs and call for help if necessary: Look for signs such as bleeding, severe abdominal pain, severe headache or visual disturbances, inability to urinate, or an urge to push prematurely. 2. Check for allergies: Always inquire about any known allergies before administering medications. 3. Administer antibiotics to the mother if indicated: If the mother has a temperature of ≥38°C, a history of foul-smelling vaginal discharge, or if the membranes have been ruptured for more than 18 hours. 4. Administer magnesium sulfate to the mother if indicated: If the diastolic blood pressure is ≥110 mmHg with 3+ proteinuria. If the diastolic blood pressure is ≥90 mmHg with 2+ proteinuria and symptoms such as severe headache, visual disturbances, or epigastric pain. 5. Administer antihypertensive medication if systolic blood pressure exceeds 160 mmHg: The goal is to maintain blood pressure below 150/100 mmHg. 6. Determine if the mother requires referral: If referral is needed, ensure it is organized promptly. 7. Start a partograph when the cervix is ≥4 cm dilated: Cervical dilation should progress at a rate of ≥1 cm per hour. Monitor and plot maternal heart rate, contractions, and fetal heart rate every 30 minutes. Record maternal temperature every 2 hours and blood pressure every 4 hours. 8. Ensure supplies are available for clean and safe delivery: Confirm the availability of gloves, hand hygiene supplies, and other essential items. 9. Encourage the presence of a birth companion: Ensure the mother or companion knows to call for help during labor if needed. 10. Prepare for delivery: For the mother: Ensure gloves, hand hygiene supplies, and oxytocin (10 units) are ready. For the baby: Have a clean towel, cord clamp or tie, sterile blade, suction device, and bag-and-mask available. Just before pushing or cesarean section: 1. Check for allergies: Confirm no known allergies before administering medications. 2. Administer antibiotics to the mother if indicated: If the mother has a temperature of ≥38°C, a history of foul-smelling vaginal discharge, membranes ruptured for >18 hours, or is undergoing a cesarean section. 3. Administer magnesium sulfate to the mother if indicated: If the diastolic blood pressure is ≥110 mmHg with 3+ proteinuria. If the diastolic blood pressure is ≥90 mmHg with 2+ proteinuria and symptoms such as severe headache, visual disturbances, or epigastric pain. 4. Administer antihypertensive medication if systolic blood pressure exceeds 160 mmHg: The goal is to maintain blood pressure below 150/100 mmHg. 5. Prepare for immediate postpartum care for the mother: Confirm it is a single baby (not multiple births). Administer oxytocin within 1 minute after birth. Deliver the placenta within 1-3 minutes after birth. Massage the uterus after the placenta is delivered and confirm uterine contraction. 6. Prepare for immediate postpartum care for the baby: Dry the baby and keep them warm. If the baby is not breathing, stimulate and clear the airway. If the baby still does not breathe, clamp and cut the cord, clear the airway if necessary, and ventilate with a bag-and-mask. Call for help immediately. Soon after birth (within 1 hour): 1. Monitor the mother for abnormal bleeding: If bleeding is abnormal, call for help, massage the uterus, consider additional uterotonics, start IV fluids, and keep the mother warm. Treat the underlying cause (e.g., uterine atony, retained placenta, vaginal tear, or uterine rupture). 2. Administer antibiotics to the mother if indicated: If the placenta was manually removed or if the mother has a temperature of ≥38°C with chills or foul-smelling vaginal discharge. 3. Administer magnesium sulfate to the mother if indicated: If the diastolic blood pressure is ≥110 mmHg with 3+ proteinuria. If the diastolic blood pressure is ≥90 mmHg with 2+ proteinuria and symptoms such as severe headache, visual disturbances, or epigastric pain. 4. Administer antihypertensive medication if systolic blood pressure exceeds 160 mmHg: The goal is to maintain blood pressure below 150/100 mmHg. 5. Monitor the baby for signs of distress: Administer antibiotics if the baby has a respiratory rate >60/min or <30/min, chest in-drawing, grunting, convulsions, poor movement on stimulation, a temperature <35°C (not rising after warming), or a temperature ≥38°C. 6. Provide special care and monitoring for the baby if indicated: If the baby was born more than 1 month early, has a birth weight <2500 grams, required resuscitation, or needs antibiotics. 7. Encourage breastfeeding and skin-to-skin contact: If the mother and baby are well, initiate breastfeeding and skin-to-skin contact. Before discharge: 1. Ensure the mother stays at the facility for at least 24 hours after delivery. 2. Assess the mother for any ongoing issues: If antibiotics, antihypertensive treatment, or other interventions are needed, delay discharge until the condition is stabilized. 3. Assess the baby for any ongoing issues: If antibiotics or special care is required, delay discharge and provide appropriate treatment. 4. Ensure the baby is feeding well: If not, establish good breastfeeding practices before discharge. 5. Discuss and offer family planning options to the mother. 6. Monitor for danger signs in the mother: These include bleeding, severe abdominal pain, severe headache or visual disturbances, breathing difficulty, fever or chills, difficulty emptying the bladder, or epigastric pain. 7. Monitor for danger signs in the baby: These include fast or difficult breathing, fever, being unusually cold, poor feeding, reduced activity, or yellowing of the whole body. Important Notes: This checklist is not comprehensive and should not replace case notes or partograph documentation. Modifications to fit local practices are encouraged.
